content.p: The Rollin' 30s Harlem Crips are a Crips set based in the Jefferson Park area of South Los Angeles, despite the New York place name in their title; federal agents described them in 2013 as a "multi-generational violent gang" and one of the Los Angeles Police Department's top targeted street gangs. The name has since turned up far from home. Federal prosecutors have charged people described as Rollin' 30s members in East Harlem, the Bronx, Roanoke in Virginia and Orlando in Florida, and the cases show a label that travels more easily than any central command.

The record is mostly prosecutors' press releases, written to announce arrests and sentences. Indictments are allegations. Where this account relies on one, it says so, and where a court has convicted someone or accepted a guilty plea, it says that too.
content.h2: A Los Angeles set with older roots
content.p: A gang-tracking website that compiles material on street gangs says the Rollin' 30s were formerly known as the Harlem Godfathers and that their history goes back to the 1960s. That site is a hobbyist compilation and carries reader comments, so its dates are not independently confirmed here. It describes territory running from Jefferson Boulevard to Martin Luther King Boulevard between Crenshaw Boulevard and Normandie Avenue, and it lists several cliques: 35th Street, 37th Street, 39th Street, the Avenues and Denker Park.

The FBI's account is narrower. In 2013 it said the gang was made up of three factions, which it called cliques or sets: the Avenues, Denker Park and 39th Street. Each claimed its own piece of the gang's overall territory and had its own leaders, or "shotcallers", who directed criminal activity. Law enforcement estimated the membership at between 700 and 1,000.

The same gang-tracking site says the set has feuded with a Bloods set, the Rollin 20s, since the 1980s, and says that conflict has cost more than a dozen young lives. Neither the FBI nor the US Attorney's Office made that claim in the pages opened here, so it rests on that one site.

On 29 August 2013, over 800 officers and federal agents served dozens of arrest and search warrants in Los Angeles. The FBI called the operation Thumbs Down, an 18-month investigation that it said began in 2012 and aimed at high-level members of the gang. The name came from the gang's hand signs, including two thumbs pointed up to stand for the "H" in Harlem.

The announcement came from US Attorney Birotte, the FBI's Los Angeles assistant director in charge Bill Lewis, LAPD Chief Charlie Beck and City Attorney Mike Feuer. Thirty-five defendants charged with federal or state offences were in custody after the morning's operation, and others were already jailed on unrelated charges or being sought as fugitives. A grand jury had returned federal indictments against 21 defendants. The counts covered crack cocaine with intent to distribute, a conspiracy to do so, a convicted felon holding a gun, running premises used for drugs, and selling firearms without a licence. Many faced mandatory minimum prison terms of five to 10 years and maximum penalties of 20 or 30 years.

Throughout the investigation and before that day, the FBI said, task force members had arrested 60 Rollin' 30s members and associates on state charges, seized 32 firearms and seized more than 10 kilograms of rock cocaine. Agents also served 34 federal search warrants. The officials put figures on the neighbourhood: 29 homicides within five years in the gang's claimed area, plus about 1,100 robberies and 1,075 assaults in the 1.5 square miles it covers. The FBI also said the gang was suspected of a series of residential "knock-knock" burglaries, which the gang itself called "floccin", and that police departments in several Southern California counties were investigating members in connection with them.

The operation was not only a drug case. Officials said the task force worked with other agencies on what the FBI called long-term community stability. The Los Angeles City Attorney's Office was pursuing property abatement, evictions and case conferences for locations it described as gang-controlled, and the Inspector General of the Department of Housing and Urban Development was looking into Section 8 housing violations that the FBI said would include the removal of tenants. Feuer said the aim was to make property owners take steps to get gang members out of their buildings. CBS Los Angeles reported that part of the investigation turned up social media photographs of very small children of gang members pointing guns at the camera.

The FBI's release carried the standard warning that an indictment holds allegations and that every defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty. The pages opened for this account do not give the outcome of the individual cases.
content.h2: Crack, a minimart and a second Los Angeles case, 2019
content.p: A later federal case, announced in a Justice Department release dated 2 October 2019, shows the gang still drawing federal attention. Six grand jury indictments charged a total of 21 defendants. Ten members and associates were arrested that day, one defendant was in state prison and another in county jail, and authorities were still looking for nine.

The main indictment charged 14 people with conspiring to manufacture and distribute crack cocaine in territory the gang claimed. It named Angelo Gabriel Reed, then 39, of Inglewood, also known as "Maniac" and "Yacc", as the gang leader. It alleged that between May 2017 and April 2018 Reed oversaw a crew that sold drugs on the street, delivered them to other distributors and customers and collected the proceeds. It further alleged that he cooked crack in his own kitchen and was involved in supplying, cooking and distributing more than 280 grams, and that some of it changed hands in front of a public library branch in Exposition Park and in a park close by.

Another indictment concerned a minimart in Exposition Park that looked closed but, according to the indictment, was widely known as a gang hangout where drugs were sold. After two undercover buys, a search warrant turned up a .40-caliber pistol, dozens of rounds of ammunition, drug paraphernalia and baggies of cocaine. These were charges, not findings. The release said that anyone convicted on all counts faced decades in prison and that some faced a mandatory minimum of 10 years.

The name also appears in New York: investigators said a group using the Rollin' 30's name had been active in Harlem since at least the middle of 1995. On 30 October 1997 the New York Times reported that 24 alleged members had been arrested the previous day in a sweep, with 63 gang members then in jail in total. Police Commissioner Howard Safir announced the end of a seven-month investigation. A 25-count indictment named 27 people and charged crimes including attempted murder, sexual assault and selling crack and heroin in East Harlem. Three other members were being sought, and police said charges in 20 unsolved homicides or shootings were possible.

According to Sgt. Louis A. Savelli of the citywide gang enforcement unit, the gang's leader, Dalmin Mayen, and his two brothers arrived from Belize more than six years earlier and set up a drug trade in the blocks around 118th Street and Fifth Avenue. Investigators told the Times that, unlike the few other Crips sets then in New York, this one had taken its name while still in Belize, after meeting Crips who had been deported from the United States, most likely from Los Angeles. They said it sold crack in little blue bags, with members in blue bandannas, and that at its height it took in up to $4,000 a day with dozens of enforcers, street sellers and lookouts. Some members drove to North Carolina to trade drugs for guns, they said.

The complaint described two incidents that drew police attention. In November 1995, according to the complaint, several members assaulted a teenage girl wearing red, the colour of the Bloods, forced her into a lobby and cut her dress off. In April 1996, it said, Mayen fired several shots at an elderly neighbour who had confronted him about selling drugs. The Times article reported these as investigators' accounts and does not say how the cases ended.

A second New York case was already pending when a superseding indictment unsealed on 22 May 2018 added five defendants, including Randy Torres, known as "Rico", to people already charged with racketeering, firearms and narcotics offences. The US Attorney's Office said the enterprise was known as the "Rollin' 30s", the "Harlem Mafia" or the "Dirt Gang". It alleged that Richard Feliz fired at a rival on 26 March 2015 and instead hit Victor Chafla, an innocent father standing outside the shop where he worked stocking fruit and vegetables. Chafla died a few days later.

In February 2020 the office announced that a jury had convicted Torres, Walston Owen and Charles Ventura of racketeering charges after a 15-day trial before Judge Victor Marrero. Owen and Ventura were also found guilty of attempted murder in aid of racketeering and related firearms offences. The jury found that Torres's part in the conspiracy included the murder of Nestor Suazo on 19 September 2015, and that Owen's included the death of Chafla. The office said a fight between Torres, other gang members and a rival Crips faction at a Bronx music video shoot came before Suazo's killing.

The sentences came in September 2022. Torres and Owen each received 39 and a half years in prison. The office said Torres, 41, described himself as "four levels from the top" of the Crips national leadership, oversaw several Crips sets and hundreds of members in New York City and elsewhere, and used a Bronx elementary school, where he worked as a maintenance worker, and its gym for gang meetings. It said Owen led the "Stratford Avenue Rollin' 30s", a Bronx subset, and ordered the shooting that killed Chafla. Derrick Richardson, who had pleaded guilty, was sentenced to 24 and a half years for shooting Suazo, running concurrently with an earlier 11-year sentence for related offences. The office said Richardson was captured on surveillance footage fleeing the scene and discarding the gun.

In Virginia, four men who were members of what prosecutors called the Roanoke set of the Rollin' 30s, centred in the Lansdowne area of northwest Roanoke, pleaded guilty to racketeering offences. On 15 August 2022 Sean Denzel Guerrant, known as "Harlem Denk", received 37 years, Demonte Rashod Mack 40 years and Trayvone Raycron Kasey 36 years. A fourth man, Chauncey Dion Levesy, was to be sentenced later.

The court record, as summarised by the US Attorney's Office, describes two killings. Guerrant admitted ordering a 17-year-old, Nickalas Lee, to kill another gang member identified as D.F. because of perceived disloyalty. On 15 June 2017 that target escaped after Lee warned him of danger. Mack then pointed his own gun at Lee and told him to hand over his weapon, and Kasey and Mack chased Lee and shot him twice in the back. Eight months later, on 9 February 2018, Kasey shot Markel Girty in the chest and took his belongings; Girty drove away but died of the wound.

In Florida, in 2018, a man identified as a member of what the Drug Enforcement Administration called the "Rolling 30s" Crips received a federal term of 10 years and 11 months for selling heroin, methamphetamine and guns to an informant in Orlando. The release said the gang had been linked to several homicides in the Orlando area.
content.h2: A name with little central control
content.p: The prosecutions describe a pattern. In Los Angeles the targets were cliques with territorial leaders. In New York, investigators said, the name arrived with immigrants who had adopted it in Belize. In the Bronx one defendant claimed rank in a national Crips structure, and in Roanoke a local set kept to its own corner of the city. Prosecutors named all of them as the Rollin' 30s, and the pages opened here do not show whether these groups answered to one another or only shared a name.
